name: True religion as 'holy folly': the rejection of theological system-building
plain_explanation: In The Praise of Folly, Erasmus suggests -- half-jokingly, half-seriously -- that genuine religion is a kind of foolishness: it comes from simple, heartfelt Christian devotion rather than from the elaborate, hair-splitting arguments of scholastic theologians about the Trinity, transubstantiation, or the minutiae of monastic rule.
precise_definition: Russell's identification of the book's underlying thesis: 'true religion is a form of Folly... the kind praised seriously is that which is displayed in Christian simplicity... the first appearance in literature... of the view... according to which true religion comes from the heart, not the head, and all elaborate theology is superfluous... essentially, a rejection of Hellenic intellectualism by the sentimentalism of the North.'
why_it_mattered: Russell credits this as an early anticipation of a view (traced forward to Rousseau's Savoyard Vicar) that becomes 'pretty generally accepted among Protestants,' making Erasmus an unlikely precursor of a broadly Protestant sentimentalist strand in religious thought, despite his ultimate opposition to the Reformation itself.
historical_origin: First articulated, so far as Russell knows, in The Praise of Folly (conceived 1509, published soon after).
examples: Folly's mock praise of pardons, indulgences, saint-worship, Trinitarian and Incarnational disputes, transubstantiation, and monastic punctilio
The imagined scene of Christ interrupting monks' self-congratulation over minor devotions to remind them of the one commandment to love one another
competing_positions: Scholastic theology's systematic, intellectualized approach to doctrine
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell links it forward to Rousseau's Savoyard Vicar and to the general Protestant tendency to prioritize heartfelt faith over dogma.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Central to Erasmus's critique of ecclesiastical abuses (popes, cardinals, bishops, monastic orders), even though he ultimately rejected Luther's schism.
